locator.text: Equation (C.16), p. 162, in the proof of Proposition C.2

provenance.note: machine audit: worker, gate, reviewer; not confirmed by a human

verdicts.summary: Lean has a weaker form of it. The paper bounds all η-derivative orders of the stress-vector difference, Σ_{j=0}^m |∂_η^j(p_{s,N} - p_s)| ≤ C_m/N, for every m. What I found in Lean is the order-0 statement only: both profile_stocks_rate declarations bound |profileStockOne (P n) - profileStockOne Q| and |profileStockTwo (P n) - profileStockTwo Q| pointwise on the compact parameter set S, with no η-derivative of the difference bounded. (Lean's two stocks are the two components of the paper's p_s: profileStockOne = X·angularLag/L and profileStockTwo = X·axialLag/(L·E).) The Lean input is one η-derivative deeper than its output — profileData carries the row values together with their first parameterPartial, and profileHistory_first_jet_bound (ModulatedStockBounds.lean:283) feeds it a FiniteJetBound 1 — which matches the paper's own remark that order m of the stocks consumes order m+1 of the histories, at m = 0 only. Severity low rather than medium because I traced the paper's two uses of (C.16) in the proof of Proposition C.2 — preserving the cone inequality between the interval 𝒥 and the first correction interval, and preserving it inside the correction interval — and both are inequalities between stock values at a point, needing only j = 0. I did not find a higher-order η-jet rate for the stocks anywhere in the modulation files; the nearest higher-order statement, ActivationStocks.log_stocks_uniform_jets (:711), is about the activation ramp parameters (T, κ), not about the N-modulation, so it is not a counterpart.
